doc.title: Phoebe Jacobs and Jackie Harris interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 21, 2006

title: Festivals versus nightclubs
summary: Jacobs and Harris debate whether festivals have replaced clubs, where unknown players get chances, and the cost of running clubs.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: I’ve got to disagree with you on one thing, Jackie. You completely forgot festivals. Look how successful festivals have been.

And festivals attract an enormous amount of people. Jazz and Heritage Festival in New Orleans, 80,000 people a day. The JVC Festival in New York, the Fest of Chicago’s has festivals. I mean all those things. I think they’ve replaced the night clubs. Instead of people going to a night club they’re going to festivals.
Well people are going to festivals which is good, and festivals are good family entertainment.
But still I think the music was really nurtured in those clubs and there is, to me, there is nothing, you know—
Well you’re right in that respect.
than going to a nightclub to see a jazz artist.
Because at a festival, at a festival you have to be a star to be hired by a festival.
And in a nightclub you could just be an up and coming performer and they’re going to give you a chance.
That’s right. And then they’ll allow, in clubs, college students can come and sit in, you know, which is good and that’s where they get their experience in performing in front of audiences.

And I don’t want to see us lose that. You know? I would really like to see us continue and you’re right because in a lot of cases a jazz artist can not get a gig at a festival if the producers do not see him as being able to attract a large number of, a large audience.
That have a name. Absolutely. You’re absolutely right. And don’t you think that the costs these days have made clubs close that normally were in abundance. © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

Really. Oh definitely. But you know when you look at, that’s a hard risk. The night club business and the restaurant business is really, really a hard business. But I really am happy to see sometimes on Sundays you will see a jazz brunch in clubs and restaurants will, especially restaurants will hire musicians which is a good thing.
